notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Himalayan rivers originate mainly in the Himalayas and adjoining highlands.
  • Major Himalayan river systems are:
  • Indus.
  • Ganga.
  • Brahmaputra.
  • Most are perennial because they receive water from:
  • Snowmelt.
  • Glaciers.
  • Rainfall.
  • They carry large quantities of water and sediments.
  • They form extensive floodplains, meanders and deltas in their lower courses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Himalayan Rivers → Perennial + Large Basins + Heavy Sediment Load

2. Perennial Rivers
  • A perennial river carries water throughout the year.
  • Himalayan rivers remain perennial because their catchments receive both monsoon rainfall and snow/glacier melt.
  • Their discharge still varies greatly by season.
3. Major Himalayan Drainage Systems

The three great Himalayan river systems are:

  • Indus River System.
  • Ganga River System.
  • Brahmaputra River System.
📌 Must-Memorise

Himalayan Drainage → Indus + Ganga + Brahmaputra

4. Antecedent Drainage
  • Some Himalayan rivers existed before the present mountain ranges reached their current elevation.
  • They maintained their original courses while the mountains were uplifted.
  • Such rivers are called antecedent rivers.
  • They cut deep gorges across mountain ranges.

Important examples include stretches of:

  • Indus.
  • Sutlej.
  • Brahmaputra.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Antecedent River → Maintains Course During Mountain Uplift

5. Himalayan Gorges
  • Rivers cut deeply into rising Himalayan ranges.
  • This produces narrow and steep-sided gorges.
  • The Indus and Brahmaputra are famous for very deep Himalayan gorges.
6. Drainage Basin
  • A drainage basin is the entire area drained by a river and its tributaries.
  • It is separated from neighbouring basins by drainage divides.
7. Tributary
  • A tributary is a smaller river that joins a larger river.
  • Himalayan systems contain numerous large tributaries.
8. Distributary
  • A distributary branches away from the main river.
  • Distributaries are common in deltaic regions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tributary → Joins

Distributary → Leaves

9. Indus River System — Overview
  • Indus is one of the great rivers of Asia.
  • It originates in the Tibetan Plateau region.
  • It flows through Ladakh and then Pakistan.
  • It finally drains into the Arabian Sea.
  • A large part of its basin lies outside present-day India.
10. Source of Indus
  • Indus rises near the Lake Manasarovar region in Tibet.
  • It is known as Sindhu in India.
  • It flows northwestward before entering Ladakh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indus = Sindhu

11. Indus in Ladakh
  • Indus flows through a deep valley in Ladakh.
  • Important tributaries join it in the high-altitude region.
  • Leh lies near the Indus valley.
12. Indus Gorge
  • The Indus cuts through high mountain terrain.
  • Near the western Himalayan syntaxis, it forms a spectacular gorge.
  • Nanga Parbat is associated with this region.
13. Main Indus Tributaries

Important tributaries include:

  • Jhelum.
  • Chenab.
  • Ravi.
  • Beas.
  • Sutlej.

These five rivers are traditionally associated with Punjab.

14. Punjab and Five Rivers
  • Punjab means "land of five waters."
  • The five major rivers are:
  • Jhelum.
  • Chenab.
  • Ravi.
  • Beas.
  • Sutlej.
📌 Must-Memorise

Punjab Five Rivers → Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej

15. Jhelum River
  • Jhelum originates in the Kashmir region.
  • Its traditional source is associated with Verinag Spring.
  • It flows through the Kashmir Valley.
  • It passes through Wular Lake.
  • It later joins the Chenab system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jhelum → Verinag → Kashmir Valley → Wular

16. Verinag
  • Verinag is a famous spring in Jammu and Kashmir.
  • It is traditionally considered the source of the Jhelum River.
17. Wular Lake and Jhelum
  • Jhelum flows through Wular Lake.
  • Wular is an important freshwater lake of Jammu and Kashmir.
18. Chenab River
  • Chenab is formed by the confluence of:
  • Chandra.
  • Bhaga.
  • The confluence occurs at Tandi in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Chenab then flows through Jammu and Kashmir before entering Pakistan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chenab = Chandra + Bhaga

19. Chandra River
  • Chandra rises in the high Himalayas of Himachal Pradesh.
  • It drains part of the Lahaul-Spiti region.
20. Bhaga River
  • Bhaga also rises in the high Himalayas.
  • It joins Chandra at Tandi.
21. Ravi River
  • Ravi rises in Himachal Pradesh.
  • It flows through the Chamba region.
  • It later enters Punjab and Pakistan.
22. Beas River
  • Beas rises near Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh.
  • It flows through Kullu Valley.
  • It joins the Sutlej in Punjab.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Beas → Near Rohtang Pass → Kullu Valley

23. Sutlej River
  • Sutlej originates in Tibet near the Lake Manasarovar-Rakshastal region.
  • It enters India through Himachal Pradesh.
  • It passes near Shipki La.
  • It is an important tributary of the Indus system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sutlej → Tibet → Shipki La Region

24. Sutlej as Antecedent River
  • Sutlej cuts across Himalayan ranges.
  • It is considered an antecedent river in important stretches.
25. Bhakra-Nangal Project
  • Bhakra Dam is built on the Sutlej River.
  • It is located in Himachal Pradesh near the Punjab border region.
  • The project supports:
  • Irrigation.
  • Hydroelectricity.
  • Water supply.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhakra Dam → Sutlej

26. Pong Dam
  • Pong Dam is built on the Beas River.
  • It is located in Himachal Pradesh.
  • The reservoir is also known as Maharana Pratap Sagar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pong Dam → Beas

27. Indus Waters Treaty
  • The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 between India and Pakistan.
  • It was brokered with the assistance of the World Bank.
  • It deals with the use of waters of the Indus river system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indus Waters Treaty → 1960 → India & Pakistan

28. Eastern and Western Rivers under Indus Treaty

Under the treaty framework:

Eastern Rivers:

  • Ravi.
  • Beas.
  • Sutlej.

Western Rivers:

  • Indus.
  • Jhelum.
  • Chenab.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Eastern → Ravi, Beas, Sutlej

Western → Indus, Jhelum, Chenab

29. Ganga River System — Overview
  • Ganga is the most important river system of northern India.
  • Its basin is the largest in India.
  • It drains a large part of northern and eastern India.
  • It eventually enters Bangladesh and reaches the Bay of Bengal.
30. Source of Ganga
  • The Ganga begins as the Bhagirathi in the Gangotri Glacier region.
  • Gaumukh is associated with the snout of Gangotri Glacier.
  • Bhagirathi meets Alaknanda at Devprayag.
  • From Devprayag onward, the river is called Ganga.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhagirathi + Alaknanda at Devprayag → Ganga

31. Gangotri Glacier
  • Gangotri Glacier lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is an important glacier of the Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Bhagirathi originates from this glacier region.
32. Gaumukh
  • Gaumukh is associated with the snout of Gangotri Glacier.
  • It is an important pilgrimage and geographical location.
33. Bhagirathi River
  • Bhagirathi is considered one of the headstreams of the Ganga.
  • It flows through Uttarakhand.
  • Tehri Dam is built on the Bhagirathi.
34. Alaknanda River
  • Alaknanda is another major headstream of the Ganga.
  • It originates in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand.
  • Several tributaries join it before Devprayag.
35. Panch Prayag

The five famous confluences in Uttarakhand are:

  • Vishnuprayag.
  • Nandprayag.
  • Karnaprayag.
  • Rudraprayag.
  • Devprayag.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panch Prayag → 5 Himalayan Confluences

36. Vishnuprayag
  • Vishnuprayag is the confluence of Alaknanda and Dhauliganga.
37. Nandprayag
  • Nandprayag is the confluence of Alaknanda and Nandakini.
38. Karnaprayag
  • Karnaprayag is the confluence of Alaknanda and Pindar.
39. Rudraprayag
  • Rudraprayag is the confluence of Alaknanda and Mandakini.
40. Devprayag
  • Devprayag is the confluence of Alaknanda and Bhagirathi.
  • From here, the river is known as Ganga.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Devprayag → Formation of Ganga

41. Tehri Dam
  • Tehri Dam is built on the Bhagirathi River.
  • It is located in Uttarakhand.
  • It is a major multipurpose project.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tehri Dam → Bhagirathi

42. Ganga Enters Plains
  • Ganga emerges from the Himalayan foothills at Haridwar.
  • From there, it enters the Northern Plains.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ganga Enters Plains → Haridwar

43. Major Ganga Tributaries

Important tributaries include:

Northern/Himalayan side:

  • Yamuna.
  • Ramganga.
  • Ghaghara.
  • Gandak.
  • Kosi.

Southern/Peninsular side:

  • Chambal.
  • Betwa.
  • Ken.
  • Son.
44. Yamuna River
  • Yamuna is the most important right-bank tributary of the Ganga.
  • It originates from the Yamunotri Glacier region in Uttarakhand.
  • It flows through or along:
  • Uttarakhand.
  • Haryana.
  • Delhi.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • It joins Ganga at Prayagraj.
📌 Must-Memorise

Yamuna → Yamunotri → Prayagraj

45. Yamunotri
  • Yamunotri lies in Uttarakhand.
  • It is associated with the source region of Yamuna.
46. Ganga-Yamuna Confluence
  • Ganga and Yamuna meet at Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh.
  • The confluence is traditionally called Triveni Sangam.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ganga + Yamuna → Prayagraj

47. Chambal River
  • Chambal rises in central India.
  • It flows through Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
  • It joins Yamuna.
  • It is famous for ravine topography.
48. Betwa River
  • Betwa originates in Madhya Pradesh.
  • It flows through Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
  • It joins Yamuna.
49. Ken River
  • Ken rises in Madhya Pradesh.
  • It flows through the Bundelkhand region.
  • It joins Yamuna.
50. Sind River
  • Sind is another tributary of Yamuna.
  • It drains parts of Madhya Pradesh.
51. Ramganga River
  • Ramganga originates in Uttarakhand.
  • It flows through the Ganga plain.
  • It joins the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh.
52. Ghaghara River
  • Ghaghara is a major Himalayan tributary of the Ganga.
  • It originates in the Tibetan-Himalayan region.
  • It flows through Nepal before entering India.
  • It is known by different names in different stretches.
53. Karnali
  • Ghaghara is known as Karnali in Nepal.
  • It is one of the major Himalayan rivers flowing into the Ganga system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karnali in Nepal → Ghaghara in India

54. Gandak River
  • Gandak originates in the Nepal Himalayas.
  • It flows southward through Nepal.
  • It enters Bihar and joins Ganga.
55. Kosi River
  • Kosi originates from several Himalayan tributaries in Tibet and Nepal.
  • It enters Bihar.
  • It has historically shifted its course extensively across the plains.
  • It is notorious for floods.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kosi → Sorrow of Bihar

56. Sapt Kosi
  • Kosi is formed by a system of seven major streams in the Himalayan region.
  • Therefore, it is often called Sapt Kosi.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kosi → Sapt Kosi

57. Why Kosi Changes Course

Reasons include:

  • Heavy sediment load.
  • Low gradient in the plains.
  • Deposition in channels.
  • Flooding.
  • Channel avulsion.
58. Son River
  • Son originates near the Amarkantak region.
  • It flows northeastward.
  • It joins the Ganga in Bihar.
  • It is a major right-bank tributary.
📌 Must-Memorise

Son → Amarkantak → Ganga

59. Gomti River
  • Gomti originates in Uttar Pradesh.
  • It flows through Lucknow.
  • It joins the Ganga.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lucknow → Gomti

60. Damodar River
  • Damodar flows through Jharkhand and West Bengal.
  • It joins the Hugli system through distributary connections.
  • It was traditionally called the Sorrow of Bengal.
61. Ganga in Uttar Pradesh

Important cities along or near the Ganga system include:

  • Haridwar.
  • Kanpur.
  • Prayagraj.
  • Varanasi.
62. Ganga in Bihar
  • Ganga flows west to east across Bihar.
  • Major tributaries entering include:
  • Ghaghara.
  • Gandak.
  • Kosi.
  • Son.
63. Ganga in West Bengal
  • In West Bengal, the Ganga divides into distributary systems.
  • One important branch is the Bhagirathi-Hugli.
  • The main eastern channel flows into Bangladesh.
64. Bhagirathi-Hugli
  • Bhagirathi-Hugli is an important distributary of the Ganga in West Bengal.
  • Kolkata lies on the Hugli River.
  • Haldia is near the lower Hugli estuarine region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kolkata → Hugli River

65. Farakka Barrage
  • Farakka Barrage is built across the Ganga in West Bengal.
  • It was designed partly to divert water toward the Bhagirathi-Hugli system.
  • It is associated with navigation and river-flow management.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Farakka Barrage → Ganga → West Bengal

66. Ganga in Bangladesh
  • After entering Bangladesh, the main Ganga channel is commonly called Padma.
  • It later joins the Brahmaputra/Jamuna system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ganga in Bangladesh → Padma

67. Meghna System
  • The combined Ganga-Brahmaputra waters eventually join the Meghna system.
  • They discharge into the Bay of Bengal through a vast delta.
68. Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta
  • It is one of the world's largest delta systems.
  • It extends across India and Bangladesh.
  • It contains numerous distributaries and tidal channels.
69. Sundarbans
  • Sundarbans occupies the lower delta.
  • It is famous for mangrove forests.
  • It extends across West Bengal and Bangladesh.
  • It is affected by tides, cyclones and river sedimentation.
70. Ganga River Length
  • Ganga is approximately 2,525 km long in standard Indian geography references.
  • It is India's longest river when measured within the conventional Indian river-system context.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ganga Length → About 2,525 km

71. Ganga Basin
  • Ganga basin is the largest river basin in India.
  • It supports a very large population.
  • It is agriculturally and culturally important.
72. Ganga Plain Agriculture

Major crops include:

  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Jute in lower basin regions.
73. Ganga Pollution

Major pollution sources include:

  • Untreated sewage.
  • Industrial effluents.
  • Solid waste.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Religious and domestic activities.
74. Ganga and Navigation
  • Ganga provides important inland-navigation opportunities.
  • Low gradients and large discharge support navigation in selected stretches.
75. Brahmaputra River System — Overview
  • Brahmaputra is one of Asia's largest rivers.
  • It originates in Tibet.
  • It flows eastward across the Tibetan Plateau.
  • It turns sharply southward around the eastern Himalayas.
  • It enters India through Arunachal Pradesh.
  • It flows through Assam and Bangladesh.
76. Brahmaputra in Tibet
  • In Tibet, Brahmaputra is called Yarlung Tsangpo or Tsangpo.
  • It flows eastward north of the main Himalayan range.
📌 Must-Memorise

Brahmaputra in Tibet → Tsangpo

77. Source Region of Brahmaputra
  • Brahmaputra rises in the Tibetan Plateau near the Himalayan region.
  • Its source is associated with glaciers in southwestern Tibet.
78. Great Bend of Brahmaputra
  • The river bends sharply around Namcha Barwa.
  • It then cuts through a deep gorge.
  • This is one of the world's major river bends.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brahmaputra Great Bend → Namcha Barwa

79. Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh
  • After entering India, the river is commonly called Siang or Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • It flows through deep valleys.
  • Major tributaries join before it enters Assam.
80. Dihang/Siang
  • Dihang or Siang is the name used for the upper Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • After meeting important tributaries, the river is known as Brahmaputra in Assam.
81. Dibang River
  • Dibang is an important tributary joining the Siang/Brahmaputra system in Arunachal Pradesh.
82. Lohit River
  • Lohit is another major eastern tributary.
  • It joins the Brahmaputra system near the Assam-Arunachal region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Siang + Dibang + Lohit → Brahmaputra System in Assam Region

83. Brahmaputra in Assam
  • Brahmaputra flows westward across Assam.
  • It occupies a broad alluvial valley.
  • It carries huge quantities of sediment.
  • Its channel is highly braided.
84. Braided River
  • A braided river divides into multiple channels separated by sandbars and islands.
  • Brahmaputra is a classic Indian example.
📌 Must-Memorise

Brahmaputra → Braided Channel

85. Majuli
  • Majuli is a famous river island in Assam.
  • It is associated with the Brahmaputra.
  • It has experienced substantial bank erosion and channel change.
📌 Must-Memorise

Majuli → Brahmaputra → Assam

86. Important Brahmaputra Tributaries

Major tributaries include:

Northern side:

  • Subansiri.
  • Kameng.
  • Manas.
  • Sankosh.

Southern side:

  • Burhi Dihing.
  • Dhansiri.
  • Kopili.
87. Subansiri River
  • Subansiri is a major tributary of Brahmaputra.
  • It flows from the Himalayan region into Assam.
88. Manas River
  • Manas is an important tributary of Brahmaputra.
  • It flows from Bhutan into Assam.
  • Manas National Park is associated with the river system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Manas River → Bhutan + Assam

89. Teesta River
  • Teesta originates in the eastern Himalayas.
  • It flows through Sikkim and West Bengal.
  • It enters Bangladesh.
  • It ultimately joins the Brahmaputra system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Teesta → Sikkim + West Bengal

90. Brahmaputra in Bangladesh
  • In Bangladesh, Brahmaputra's main lower channel is commonly called Jamuna.
  • It joins the Padma.
📌 Must-Memorise

Brahmaputra in Bangladesh → Jamuna

91. Padma-Jamuna Confluence
  • Padma carries Ganga waters.
  • Jamuna carries Brahmaputra waters.
  • Their combined flow later joins the Meghna system before entering the Bay of Bengal.
92. Brahmaputra Floods
  • Brahmaputra is highly flood-prone.
  • Reasons include:
  • Heavy monsoon rainfall.
  • Himalayan snowmelt.
  • Large sediment load.
  • Channel migration.
  • Tributary floods.
  • Earthquake-induced sediment changes.
93. Bank Erosion in Assam
  • Riverbank erosion is severe along the Brahmaputra.
  • Villages, farmland and infrastructure may be lost.
  • River islands constantly change shape.
94. Brahmaputra Sediment Load
  • Young Himalayan rocks erode rapidly.
  • Tributaries bring large quantities of sediments.
  • Deposition causes sandbars and channel instability.
95. Ganga vs Brahmaputra Channel

Ganga:

  • More stable in many plains stretches.
  • Meandering channels common.

Brahmaputra:

  • Very high sediment load.
  • Braided channels common.
  • Greater channel instability.
96. Indus vs Ganga vs Brahmaputra Outlets
  • Indus → Arabian Sea.
  • Ganga → Bay of Bengal through Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
  • Brahmaputra → Bay of Bengal through combined delta system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indus → Arabian Sea

Ganga/Brahmaputra → Bay of Bengal

97. Himalayan River Characteristics

Typical characteristics include:

  • Large drainage basins.
  • Perennial flow.
  • Long courses.
  • Deep mountain gorges.
  • Extensive floodplains.
  • High sediment load.
  • Large tributary networks.
98. Upper Course of Himalayan Rivers

Upper courses show:

  • Steep gradients.
  • Rapid flow.
  • Vertical erosion.
  • Gorges.
  • Rapids.
  • Waterfalls in tributary regions.
99. Middle Course

Middle courses often show:

  • Decreasing gradient.
  • Wider valleys.
  • More lateral erosion.
  • Larger tributary junctions.
100. Lower Course

Lower courses show:

  • Low gradients.
  • Meanders.
  • Floodplains.
  • Natural levees.
  • Oxbow lakes.
  • Distributaries.
  • Deltas.
101. Meanders
  • Meanders are winding river bends.
  • They are common where gradients are low.
  • Outer bends are eroded.
  • Inner bends receive deposition.
102. Oxbow Lakes
  • Oxbow lakes form when a meander loop is cut off.
  • They are common on mature floodplains.
103. Natural Levees
  • Natural levees are raised river banks formed by repeated flood deposition.
  • Coarser sediment settles near the channel.
104. Floodplains
  • Floodplains are flat low-lying areas adjacent to rivers.
  • They receive sediment during floods.
  • They are fertile but flood-prone.
105. River Terraces
  • River terraces are step-like surfaces above present floodplains.
  • They represent former valley-floor or floodplain levels.
106. Alluvial Fans
  • Himalayan streams deposit coarse sediments where they emerge onto plains.
  • Such fan-shaped deposits occur near mountain fronts.
107. Bhabar Link
  • Coarse sediments deposited along the Himalayan foothills form the Bhabar belt.
  • Streams often disappear into porous deposits.
108. Terai Link
  • South of Bhabar, streams re-emerge.
  • This creates marshy Terai conditions.
109. Himalayan Rivers and Northern Plains
  • The Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems built the Northern Plains.
  • Repeated sediment deposition created deep alluvial soils.
110. Himalayan Rivers and Agriculture

They support:

  • Irrigation.
  • Fertile alluvial soils.
  • Multiple cropping.
  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Jute.
111. Himalayan Rivers and Hydropower
  • Mountain gradients provide large hydropower potential.
  • Dams and run-of-river projects have been constructed across several tributaries.
112. Himalayan Rivers and Navigation
  • Navigation is difficult in steep upper courses.
  • Lower Ganga and Brahmaputra stretches are more suitable for inland navigation.
113. Himalayan Rivers and Flood Hazards

Flood risk is high because of:

  • Heavy monsoon rain.
  • Snowmelt.
  • Large sediment loads.
  • Channel migration.
  • Flat floodplains.
114. Riverbank Erosion
  • Strong currents attack outer river banks.
  • High-flow events accelerate erosion.
  • Brahmaputra and Kosi regions are especially affected.
115. Avulsion
  • Avulsion is sudden abandonment of a river channel in favour of a new course.
  • It can occur when sediment raises the river bed or during major floods.
  • Kosi has historically shown major course shifts.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Avulsion → Sudden River Course Shift

116. River Capture
  • River capture occurs when one river diverts the headwaters of another.
  • It is also called stream piracy.
  • Tectonic uplift and erosion can promote such drainage changes.
117. Water Divide
  • A water divide is elevated land separating two drainage basins.
  • The Himalayas and plateau uplands form major divides.
118. River Regime
  • River regime refers to seasonal variation in river discharge.
  • Himalayan rivers have more sustained flow than most peninsular rivers because of snow and glacier melt.
119. Snowmelt Contribution
  • Snowmelt increases river discharge during warmer months.
  • Its importance varies among Himalayan basins.
120. Glacier Contribution
  • Glacier melt supplements river flow.
  • Monsoon rainfall, however, remains a major contributor to annual discharge in many Himalayan basins.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Himalayan Rivers Are Not Supplied Only by Glaciers.

121. Climate Change and Himalayan Rivers

Possible impacts include:

  • Glacier retreat.
  • Changed snowmelt timing.
  • Altered river flow seasonality.
  • Greater glacial lake hazards.
  • Changes in extreme rainfall.
122. GLOF
  • GLOF means Glacial Lake Outburst Flood.
  • It occurs when water stored in a glacial lake is suddenly released.
  • Himalayan valleys are vulnerable.
123. River Pollution

Major Himalayan/plain river pollution sources include:

  • Urban sewage.
  • Industrial effluents.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Solid waste.
124. River Conservation

Important approaches include:

  • Sewage treatment.
  • Industrial effluent control.
  • Wetland protection.
  • Riverbank management.
  • Floodplain conservation.
  • Environmental-flow maintenance.
125. Environmental Flow
  • Environmental flow is the quantity, timing and quality of water needed to maintain river ecosystems and dependent human livelihoods.
  • Excessive diversion can alter ecological functioning.
126. Dams and River Systems

Dams may provide:

  • Hydropower.
  • Irrigation.
  • Flood moderation.
  • Drinking water.

But can also alter:

  • Sediment movement.
  • Fish migration.
  • Floodplain connectivity.
  • Downstream flow.
127. Sediment Trapping
  • Reservoirs trap river sediments.
  • Downstream areas may receive less sediment.
  • This can affect floodplains and deltas.
128. Delta Subsidence Risk
  • Reduced sediment supply can contribute to delta vulnerability.
  • Sea-level rise and groundwater extraction may further increase risk.
129. Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta Vulnerability

The delta is vulnerable to:

  • Cyclones.
  • Storm surges.
  • Floods.
  • River erosion.
  • Salinity.
  • Sea-level rise.
130. Important River-City Pairings
  • Srinagar → Jhelum.
  • Delhi → Yamuna.
  • Agra → Yamuna.
  • Prayagraj → Ganga-Yamuna confluence.
  • Varanasi → Ganga.
  • Kanpur → Ganga.
  • Patna → Ganga.
  • Kolkata → Hugli.
  • Guwahati → Brahmaputra.
131. Important River-Lake Pairings

136. Tamil Nadu Comparison Link
  • Himalayan rivers are generally perennial.
  • Most Tamil Nadu rivers are more rainfall-dependent and seasonal.
  • Tamil Nadu therefore relies heavily on:
  • Monsoon rainfall.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Tanks.
  • Inter-state river flows.
  • Peninsular rivers will be covered in the next chapter.
137. Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra Comparison

Indus:

  • Flows mainly toward Arabian Sea.
  • Large basin extends into Pakistan.
  • Major Punjab tributaries.

Ganga:

  • Largest basin in India.
  • Dense population and agriculture.
  • Major deltaic system.

Brahmaputra:

  • Very high sediment load.
  • Braided channel.
  • Severe floods and bank erosion.
